strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: Dynamic manipulation presents fundamentally different spatiotemporal challenges than static manipulation, with clear real-world relevance

High-quality dataset contribution: DOMINO is comprehensively designed with 117K trajectories, 5 embodiments, hierarchical complexity (3 levels), dual-task taxonomy (interception/tracking), and rigorous spatiotemporal synchronization pipeline

Rigorous experimental methodology: Comprehensive baseline comparisons (9+ SOTA methods), thorough ablations, clever oracle experiment (Table 2) isolating the historical-vs-future bottleneck, and real-world validation demonstrating sim-to-real transfer

Insightful analysis of VLA limitations: Finding 1 demonstrates architectural inadequacy (not just data); Finding 2 shows future trajectories alone insufficient without history; cross-difficulty generalization (Table 5) and task-type breakdown (Table 4) provide nuanced understanding

Technical completeness and practical considerations: Efficient inference (9.6 Hz, negligible overhead), caching strategies, LoRA adaptation, extensive supplementary material with per-task results and implementation details
Dynamic-to-static generalization evidence (Finding 3): Demonstrates that dynamic training provides robust spatiotemporal priors benefiting static tasks, supported by 4.91% co-training gain
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of PUMA: Optical flow + auxiliary future prediction is relatively straightforward; 'world queries' mechanism lacks clear mechanistic explanation; insufficient exploration of alternative motion encodings or comparison with concurrent VLA temporal reasoning methods

Concerning absolute performance severely limits utility: 17.2% SR on Level 1, 10.5% on Level 2, 4.6% on Level 3 despite labeling as 'state-of-the-art'; insufficient analysis of whether low performance reflects fundamental problem complexity or addressable gaps

Uneven experimental evaluation: Main results heavily emphasize Level 1 (linear motion); Levels 2-3 results use only 5-task subset, weakening generalization claims; real-world validation limited to 5 tasks with artificial linear string-based motion not representative of claimed deployment scenarios

Dataset limitations underexplored: Entirely simulation-based (SAPIEN) with unquantified sim-to-real gap; kinematic objects with stop-on-contact simplifies physics (no momentum, post-contact dynamics); rigid bodies only; limited to tabletop manipulation; polynomial trajectory constraints may not capture real-world stochasticity

Methodological vulnerabilities in supervision: GroundingDINO+SAM2 detection assumes perfect grounding—real deployment would fail with occlusions, novel objects, or detection failures; requires object names from language instructions, reducing open-world applicability; future supervision only during training

Incomplete generalization analysis: No systematic domain randomization ablation; cross-embodiment generalization untested (Aloha-AgileX for simulation vs. Piper for real-world); object size/shape diversity not explored; co-training benefits (Table 6) are task-dependent with minimal gains on some tasks

Presentation overclaiming: 'State-of-the-art' misleading with 17% success rate; 'dynamic-aware' is vague; Finding 3 claim about 'robust spatiotemporal representations' not fully supported (mixed results across tasks); critical implementation details (e.g., optical flow caching) relegated to appendix

Missing comparisons and engagement: Limited discussion of dynamics prediction literature, control theory, or physics-informed approaches; no comparison with forward dynamics models or action-conditioned video prediction; insufficient justification for optical flow over alternatives

Reproducibility gaps: No explicit code availability statement; hyperparameter choices (4 world queries, λ=0.05) lack justification; no statistical significance testing or error bars reported for main results; unclear if any DOMINO tasks appear in VLA pretraining

strengths: Well-motivated benchmark addressing genuinely underexplored problem: dynamic object manipulation. Figure 1 clearly demonstrates dramatic performance degradation of SOTA VLAs (44.8% → 10.9%) when objects move.

Comprehensive DOMINO dataset design: 117K trajectories, 35 tasks, 5 embodiments, hierarchical complexity levels (L1-3), parameterized dynamics coefficient, dual interception/tracking taxonomy with rigorous evaluation metrics (SR, MS, RC).
Novel three-stage spatiotemporal synchronization data collection methodology elegantly solves the challenge of acquiring expert demonstrations with synchronized moving objects and robotic actions.

Systematic and insightful analysis: Oracle experiment (Table 2) cleanly isolates that future trajectories help tracking quality (MS +30%) but not success without historical grounding—motivating the need for both history and prediction (Findings 1-2).

PUMA architecture is principle-driven by failure analysis rather than ad-hoc. Direct integration of optical flow for scene-centric history and learnable world queries for object-centric prediction yields 6.3% absolute improvement with negligible inference overhead.

Extensive experimental validation: 9+ baselines, thorough ablations (history length, prediction horizon, cross-level transfer), data scaling analysis showing PUMA benefits more from additional data, real-world sim-to-real transfer on bimanual platform (42% vs <10% baseline).
Real-world robot experiments demonstrate practical applicability beyond simulation, with LoRA fine-tuning enabling sim-to-real transfer on AgileX Piper platform.
Clear presentation with effective motivation, well-designed figures, thorough supplementary materials (implementation details, per-task breakdowns, failure analysis), and comprehensive related work.
Cross-domain insights: Finding 3 that dynamic training produces robust spatiotemporal representations transferring to static tasks is valuable for practitioners planning training data composition.

Strong generalization analysis: cross-difficulty evaluation (Table 13), dynamic coefficient robustness (Table 14), and quantification of performance degradation across complexity levels (Fig. 4) provide practical guidance.
weaknesses: Limited real-world validation: only 5 of 35 DOMINO tasks evaluated on physical robots. Real-world setup uses string-pulled objects—highly artificial compared to actual conveyor belts or interactive scenarios. Only 50 demonstrations per task for real-world training raises questions about sample efficiency.

Restrictive scope of modeled dynamics: objects follow predefined trajectories, no learned physics, stop-on-contact simplification avoids contact dynamics. No deformable objects, multi-target interactions, or friction effects. Level 3 'stochastic' dynamics still deterministic trajectory segments. Limits applicability to real assembly scenarios.

Low absolute performance levels: PUMA achieves only 17.2% SR on Level 1 (linear motion), concerning for deployment. Sharp performance cliffs across complexity (Level 2→3: 10.5%→4.6%, Table 5). Real-world 42% average is modest and tested on only 5 tasks.

Generalization concerns: training primarily on Level 1; cross-level transfer requires LoRA adaptation (not zero-shot). Table 14 shows brittleness to dynamic coefficient changes. Dynamic-to-static transfer (Table 19) produces mixed results, somewhat undermining Finding 3.

Moderate architectural novelty: optical flow encoding via Farneback is standard; auxiliary future prediction loss is known regularization. No ablation on frozen vs. learnable DINO, no comparison with frame differencing or learned optical flow. World query design lacks deep justification.

Missing ablations and analysis: no investigation of PUMA's learned optical flow patterns or failure modes when flow is ambiguous. No visualization of learned representations. Failure mode listing (Appendix F.1) lacks quantitative analysis. Why does co-training help so much (Table 6)?

Experimental rigor: no confidence intervals or significance tests; some improvements modest (17.2% vs 10.86% = 6.3 pp); baseline re-implementations with different backbones complicate attribution; evaluation metric choices (MS penalties, RC definition) lack sensitivity analysis.

Reproducibility: code marked 'TBA'; hyperparameter choices (λ=0.05) lack justification; RoboTwin 2.0/SAPIEN specificity may limit external reproducibility. Historical frame stride (4) and count (4) not sensitivity-analyzed.

Oracle experiment insight incomplete: conclusion that 'trajectory + no history causes control jitter' is plausible but lacks depth. Why doesn't future trajectory information help success rate more fundamentally? Not thoroughly investigated.

Temporal dynamics limitations: no discussion of robustness to velocity/acceleration discontinuities, occlusion handling, or failure cases when GroundingDINO/SAM2 misidentify targets. Farneback optical flow reliability with large/ambiguous motion not addressed.
